newsitem.title: USA: Talk of Bergsten joining Clinton team hurts dollar.
newsitem.headline: Talk of Bergsten joining Clinton team hurts dollar.

text.p: Press speculation that the Clinton administration is considering economist Fred Bergsten, an advocate of a weak dollar, for a top job in the White House sent the dollar tumbling against the yen Thursday, traders said.

The dollar subsequently hit a session low against the yen after a large North American money fund, rumoured to be that of influential global investor George Soros, heavily bought yen while selling German marks and Swiss francs.
A spokesman at Soros Funds declined to comment on the market rumour.
An article in the Journal of Commerce newspaper reported Bergsten was in line to replace Laura Tyson to head the National Economic Council.

Bergsten currently heads the Institute for International Economics in Washington. In the past he has triggered major dollar sell-offs against the yen by publically stating the exchange rate should drop below 100.
An advocate of a weak dollar, he previously served in the Treasury Department under President Jimmy Carter.

"The fact is that he's a consummate bear (on the dollar). When that news got out into the market, everyone started to sell dollar/yen fairly hard," said James Powers, vice president in foreign exchange sales and advisory at Westdeutsche Landesbank.
The dollar fell from above 111.60 yen to a low of 111.14. It barely recovered by the close to end at 111.21, but still lower than Wednesday's 111.75 close.

"He's an advocate of using the devaluation of the dollar to try to cure the trade deficit. So the market would view as very suspicious any attempt to try to install him as an adviser to the White House or, even worse, in the Commerce or Treasury Department," said Stephen Jury, chief dealer at Union Bank of Switzerland in New York.

Against the mark, the dollar was bolstered by supportive comments from Bundesbank officials, especially President Hans Tietmeyer, who said the dollar could go higher and that he welcomes the recent dollar rally.
"The Bundesbank was quite active today in jawboning the dollar higher. When Tietmeyer speaks, that really creates a trading environment," Powers said.
Tietmeyer reversed a four-day series of dollar losses against the mark on Tuesday when he said the dollar was on its way back up, a move he welcomed.
The dollar received a small boost in late trading after Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reiterated his support for a strong dollar.

Rubin's recent silence regarding dollar policy despite a flurry of comments from Japanese and German finance officials regarding appropriate dollar trading levels had some market players speculating the U.S. stance might change.
The dollar closed higher at 1.5085 marks, compared with 1.5077 marks at Wednesday's close.
However, a comment from Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke capped the dollar's rise against the mark.
Welteke told a news agency he feared Germany and France in 1997 might not meet the budget deficit goals in the Maastricht treaty for a proposed single European currency in 1999.
"The fact that Welteke said Germany and France may fail the criteria was a little bit alarming, but is now being discounted as something we will look at in a couple of years' time," Jury said.
The dollar continued its fall versus the British pound after hitting its lowest closing level against sterling since October 1992 on Wednesday.
Fresh British price data Thursday indicated a stronger British economy and the likelihood of higher interest rates.
Rising British rates would increase returns on investments in pound-denominated assets.
Investors flocked to the pound Wednesday after a report showed unemployment in the United Kingdom fell to 7.2 percent in October, its lowest point in nearly six years.
Sterling closed at $1.6650, up from $1.6605 on Wednesday.
In other trading, the dollar closed at 1.2745 Swiss francs and Canadian $1.3363, up from 1.2710 Swiss francs and C$1.3340 at Wednesday's close.
